entries.name: Personal & Professional Development
entries.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

entries.name: Modern History
entries.text: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.

entries.name: Histories of Gender
entries.text: Studies gender, storytelling and marginalised lives in the nineteenth- to twenty-first-century American context. Students examine slavery, community activism, representation and lived experience, using sources and projects that connect historical interpretation with contemporary questions.

entries.name: History of Empires
entries.text: History of Empires examines empires across global history and competing theories of empire. Students study expansion, administration, military and economic systems, legitimacy, ideology, culture, decline and legacies. Historical cases, source analysis and an independent research essay connect theoretical interpretation with specific imperial experiences.

entries.name: Ways of War
entries.text: Provides a chronological overview of warfare in the Western world from antiquity to the present. Covers weapons, technology, strategy, defence, mercenaries, cavalry, chivalry, Blitzkrieg, guerrilla warfare and nuclear arsenals, illustrating competition for mastery in Western history.

entries.name: Native American Histories
entries.text: Native American Histories studies Indigenous social and cultural histories from the nineteenth century to the present. Boarding schools, institutional violence, family separation and intergenerational trauma are connected to resistance, resurgence, food sovereignty and cultural expression. Storytelling, reciprocity and relational accountability guide collaboration with Indigenous peers and knowledge holders through arts-based work and a public-history project.

entries.name: Introduction to Western Philosophy
entries.text: Introduces central themes from Western philosophy over 2,500 years. Encourages inquiry into the significance of philosophical issues and their relation to other disciplines and teaches theoretical methods used by philosophers.

entries.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
entries.text: Introduction to Political Philosophy examines political thought from classical antiquity to contemporary debates, including European and non-European thinkers. Students study views of human nature, society, rights and authority in historical context and compare their arguments with current political problems. Original texts, an essay and a group project develop interpretation and normative argument.

entries.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
entries.text: Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.

entries.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
entries.text:
In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece, when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so, the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century.


Ancient commentators criticised Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion. They argued that many were too uneducated, too emotional, and too irrational to see through the cheap play on emotions by demagogues and would-be tyrants.


This course investigates how Athenian democracy was built, how it was intertwined with myth and religion, and expressed in art, literature and architecture. It traces the loci of democracy in archaeology, and analyses its temporary collapse in the crisis of the late fifth century BC. Most importantly, we put ourselves in our socio-political ancestors’ shoes by engaging in a simulation of the Athenian assembly, in which we have to make decisions that will change our lives forever. In doing so, we use the ancient heritage of democracy for an experiment in applied sociology – to not only understand, but to feel the meaning of political decision-making.

entries.name: Writing Art's Histories
entries.text: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.

A research paper, graphic explanation and creative retelling connect interpretation with narrative practice.

entries.name: Perspectives on Literary Meaning
entries.text: Examines how different perspectives—humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural minority and psychoanalytic—affect reading and interpretation. Students undertake a research project applying selected perspectives to texts.

entries.name: Introduction to Film & Media

Film history connects early cinema and major movements with feminist and postcolonial interpretation, alongside television, digital platforms and spectatorship. An analytical or creative-analytical project combines close analysis, theory and scholarly research.

entries.name: From T.V. to TikTok

Students compare dominant portrayals with Indigenous self-representation, investigate disability representation, and develop futures-oriented creative projects.
